questions.q: In SSIS, what's the fundamental difference between the Control Flow and the Data Flow?
options: Control Flow orchestrates tasks and their order/conditions; Data Flow moves and transforms rows between a source and a destination
Control Flow only runs on a schedule; Data Flow runs on demand
Data Flow is for SSRS reports; Control Flow is for SSIS packages
They're two names for the same thing
questions.explain: The Control Flow is the package's task-level workflow (Execute SQL, containers, precedence), and a Data Flow Task inside it is where actual row-by-row data movement and transformation happens — one Control Flow can contain several Data Flow tasks.

questions.q: What is an SSIS "package"?
options: The single unit of work — a .dtsx file containing the control flow, data flows, connections, and variables for one ETL job
A compressed .zip of all SSIS projects
A SQL Server database backup file
A Power BI dataset
questions.explain: A package (.dtsx) is the deployable, executable unit in SSIS — everything needed to run one ETL process lives inside it.

questions.q: What does a Precedence Constraint control in the Control Flow?
options: Whether the next task runs, based on the previous task's success, failure, or completion
The order columns appear in a Data Flow
Which server a package deploys to
How many rows a Data Flow processes at once
questions.explain: Precedence constraints are the arrows between Control Flow tasks — they can be set to Success, Failure, or Completion, controlling exactly when downstream tasks are allowed to run.

questions.q: What's a For Each Loop Container used for?
options: Repeating a set of tasks once per item in a collection, such as one file per iteration in a folder
Running a task exactly once
Pausing a package until a condition is true
Encrypting connection strings
questions.explain: A For Each Loop Container iterates its contained tasks over an enumerator — a common pattern is looping once per file in a folder, assigning the current filename to a variable each pass.

questions.q: In the Data Flow, what does a Source component do?
options: Reads rows from an external location, such as a table, file, or query, into the Data Flow's pipeline
Writes the final rows to their destination
Sorts rows before they're loaded
Validates data types only
questions.explain: A Source (OLE DB Source, Flat File Source, etc.) is where rows enter the Data Flow pipeline — everything downstream operates on the rows it reads.

questions.q: Why does SSIS process Data Flow rows in buffers rather than one row at a time?
options: Processing rows in batches (buffers) is dramatically more efficient than row-by-row processing
Buffers are required by SQL Server licensing
SSIS can only read one buffer's worth of data total per package
Buffers only apply to flat file sources
questions.explain: SSIS's Data Flow engine is a pipeline architecture that moves rows through memory buffers in batches — this batched, in-memory approach is what makes it so much faster than row-at-a-time processing.

questions.q: What does a Lookup transformation do in a Data Flow?
options: Matches incoming rows against a reference dataset and adds columns from the match, or flags no-match rows
Sorts the incoming rows alphabetically
Removes duplicate rows automatically
Converts data types on every column
questions.explain: Lookup is the classic "enrich this row with data from elsewhere" transformation — it joins each incoming row against a reference table/query and either passes matched columns through or routes no-match rows to an error/no-match output.

questions.q: What's the purpose of a Conditional Split transformation?
options: Routes rows to different outputs based on an expression, similar to a CASE/switch statement
Splits one column into two columns
Divides the Data Flow across multiple servers
Removes rows that fail a checksum
questions.explain: Conditional Split evaluates an expression per row and sends it down one of several possible outputs — the Data Flow equivalent of an IF/ELSE IF chain.

questions.q: What does an Aggregate transformation let you do inside a Data Flow?
options: Compute SUM, COUNT, AVG, MIN, MAX and GROUP BY-style groupings on rows as they pass through
Merge two Data Flows into one
Cache lookup reference data in memory
Encrypt sensitive columns
questions.explain: Aggregate is the Data Flow's answer to GROUP BY — it computes standard aggregate functions across groups of rows as they stream through the pipeline.

questions.q: What's the difference between an SSIS variable and an SSIS parameter?
options: Parameters are set from outside the package at run time; variables are typically set and used internally during execution
They're identical in every way
Variables can only hold numbers; parameters can hold any type
Parameters can't be used in expressions
questions.explain: Parameters are the package's external "inputs" — a caller (a SQL Agent job, a parent package, dtexec) can supply their values at execution time; variables are the package's own internal working values, typically set inside the package itself.

questions.q: What does an SSIS expression like @[User::FilePath] + "\\" + @[User::FileName] do?
options: Concatenates two variable values into a single string at run time
Declares two new variables
Compares two variables for equality
Deletes the file at that path
questions.explain: SSIS expressions use + as the string concatenation operator, and @[Namespace::VariableName] syntax to reference a variable — this expression builds a full file path string from two variables.

questions.q: What does an Event Handler in SSIS let you respond to?
options: Package or task-level events such as OnError, OnWarning, or OnTaskFailed
Only successful completions
Changes to source data only
Only scheduled trigger events
questions.explain: Event Handlers attach their own mini-workflow to specific lifecycle events (OnError, OnPreExecute, OnTaskFailed, etc.) on a package, container, or task — commonly used to log errors or send notifications.

questions.q: Why would you route a Data Flow's error output to a separate destination instead of letting the package fail?
options: It lets bad rows be captured and logged for review while good rows continue processing
It's required by SQL Server
It automatically fixes the bad rows
It disables logging for that component
questions.explain: Every Data Flow component has a configurable error output — redirecting failing rows there, instead of failing the whole component, lets you keep processing good rows while still capturing what went wrong with the bad ones.

questions.q: What problem does a Script Component in the Data Flow solve that built-in transformations can't?
options: It lets you write custom .NET code for logic too complex or specific for any standard transformation
It replaces the need for a Source component
It's only used for logging
It converts SSIS packages to Python scripts
questions.explain: When no built-in transformation fits (complex parsing, custom business rules, calling an external library), the Script Component drops you into real C#/VB.NET code operating on the pipeline buffer row by row.

questions.q: What's a common reason to use a Sequence Container around a group of Control Flow tasks?
options: To group related tasks logically and apply shared properties, like a transaction, to all of them at once
To make tasks run in parallel automatically
To encrypt the tasks inside it
To convert Control Flow tasks into a Data Flow
questions.explain: A Sequence Container groups tasks for organization and lets you apply container-level settings — like a shared transaction option — to everything inside it as a unit.

questions.q: What's the difference between the Project Deployment Model and the legacy Package Deployment Model in SSIS?
options: Project Deployment deploys an entire .ispac project with shared parameters/connection managers to the SSIS Catalog; Package Deployment deploys individual .dtsx files
They produce identical deployment artifacts
Package Deployment is required for Azure-SSIS
Project Deployment doesn't support parameters
questions.explain: The modern Project Deployment Model packages an entire project, with shared, environment-driven parameters and connection managers, into one .ispac file deployed to the SSIS Catalog (SSISDB) — the older model deploys .dtsx packages individually with no shared catalog.

questions.q: What is an SSIS Environment, in the SSIS Catalog, used for?
options: Storing a named set of parameter values, such as Dev vs. Prod connection strings, that a project execution can be mapped to
Encrypting the SSISDB database
A folder for storing .dtsx files only
A monitoring dashboard
questions.explain: An Environment in the SSIS Catalog holds a set of variable values — like different connection strings for Dev/Test/Prod — that you map to a project's parameters at execution time, without touching the deployed project itself.

questions.q: In a typical SSIS capstone ETL package, what's the usual high-level order of operations?
options: Extract from source(s), transform/cleanse in the Data Flow, load into the destination/warehouse, then log the run
Load first, then extract, then transform
Transform the destination table directly with no extraction step
Log the run before any data moves
questions.explain: ETL's own name describes the order: Extract source rows, Transform them in the Data Flow (lookups, conditional splits, aggregates), then Load into the destination — with logging typically wrapping the whole run via event handlers or an Execute SQL logging step.

questions.q: Why is it good practice to make an SSIS load step idempotent, i.e. safe to re-run, rather than always appending blindly?
options: If the package fails partway and is re-run, an idempotent load won't create duplicate rows
Idempotent loads run faster than any other kind
SQL Server requires all loads to be idempotent
It removes the need for error handling entirely
questions.explain: ETL packages fail and get re-run in the real world — a load designed to be safely repeatable, like a truncate-and-reload staging table or an upsert/MERGE into the target, avoids the duplicate-row mess a naive blind-append would create on a re-run.

questions.q: What's the value of adding row-count logging, such as rows extracted, loaded, and rejected, to a package?
options: It gives you an auditable, at-a-glance way to confirm a run moved the expected amount of data and catch silent failures
It's only useful for billing purposes
It replaces the need for error handling
SSIS requires it to run at all
questions.explain: A silent failure — a source returning 0 rows, or a filter accidentally dropping most of the data — won't always throw an error. Logging row counts per run gives you a simple, auditable signal to catch exactly that kind of problem quickly.
